warmup.q: A loader thread runs registry.current = new RateCard("EUR", fees); where current is a plain field and RateCard's fields are plain too. A request thread reads registry.current and gets a non-null card. What can card.currency() return?
options: Always "EUR": the constructor finished before the reference was stored
null, until the loader thread ends
warmup.why: Without an edge, the store of the reference and the stores inside the constructor may become visible in any order. A reader can see the reference before the field write, so it may read the default value, null. Program order in the loader (option 1) says nothing about what another thread sees.

sections.h: Publishing an object is a write, and it can race
sections.html:
Publishing an object means making a reference to it reachable from another thread: storing it in a shared field, a static, a collection, or handing it to code that runs elsewhere.

Java
RateCard card = new RateCard("EUR", fees);   // 1. allocate, 2. run the constructor
registry.current = card;                     // 3. publish: store the reference where others look
Kotlin
val card = RateCard("EUR", fees)             // 1. allocate, 2. run the constructor
registry.current = card                      // 3. publish: store the reference where others look

Three things happen. The JVM allocates memory with every field at its default (0, false, null). The constructor writes the fields. Then the reference is stored. In the writing thread they happen in that order. A thread that reads current through a plain field has no edge to any of them. The JIT may store the reference before the field writes, and an ARM CPU may make the stores visible in any order. So the reader can see current != null and still read a null currency or a fee of 0. That's a partially constructed object, and no line you wrote creates one.

It's not theory. The jcstress sample BasicJMM_08_Finals publishes an object with four plain int fields through a plain field. On x86_64 a reader saw the reference with some fields still 0 in about 18,000 out of 219 million samples. On AArch64 it saw just about every mix of zeros and real values.

Unsafe publication has a second failure you already know from lesson 1 of this track: the reader may never see the reference at all, because the JIT may read the field once. That's the RateCardRegistry bug in the lab.

There are two ways out. Publish through something that creates a happens-before edge, so the reference and the state travel together. Or make the object safe to see even through a race, which is what final fields do. The best code does both.

Check yourself: lesson 1 of this track showed that x86 only lets a later read pass an earlier write, so its stores reach memory in order. Yet the x86_64 run of BasicJMM_08_Finals still saw half-built objects. Which layer did that? The JIT, the only one left. It may move the field stores after the store of the reference, or move the reader's loads, and the CPU then runs them in the order the JIT chose.

video.title: Publishing is a write: a reader can see the reference before the constructor's field writes, unless an edge or final fields stop it

sections.html:
An object is safely published when the reference and the state it had at that moment reach the reader together. The standard idioms, from Java Concurrency in Practice:

  1. Initialize it in a static initializer. The JVM runs class initialization under a lock, and every thread that uses the class sees the result.
  2. Store it in a volatile field or an AtomicReference.
  3. Store it in a final field of an object that is itself properly constructed.
  4. Store it in a field guarded by a lock, or hand it over through java.util.concurrent: a concurrent map or queue, an executor, a future.

Each gives the reader an edge you already know: the class-initialization lock, volatile write and read, the final-field rule (next section), the monitor rule, or a j.u.c handoff.

Java
class RateCardRegistry {
    static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard("EUR", Map.of("VISA", 120L));         // 1. static initializer
    private volatile RateCard current = DEFAULT;                                      // 2. volatile field
    private final ConcurrentMap<String, RateCard> byCurrency = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // 4. j.u.c handoff

    void publish(RateCard card) {
        current = card;
        byCurrency.put(card.currency(), card);
    }
}
Kotlin
class RateCardRegistry {
    companion object {
        val DEFAULT = RateCard("EUR", mapOf("VISA" to 120L))   // 1. static initializer (companion object)
    }
    @Volatile private var current: RateCard = DEFAULT           // 2. @Volatile property
    private val byCurrency = ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateCard>()   // 4. j.u.c handoff

    fun publish(card: RateCard) {
        current = card
        byCurrency[card.currency] = card
    }
}

A Kotlin companion object is initialized when its class is loaded, with the same semantics as a Java static initializer, so idiom 1 works the same way.

For anything you replace at runtime, use a volatile field or an AtomicReference. Use static final for constants. Don't add synchronized getters only to publish; a volatile read is cheaper and says what you mean.

Safe publication covers the state the object had when you published it. If you change the object afterwards, each change needs its own synchronization. That's why the best objects to publish are the ones that never change.

try.title: Safe or not?
steps: For each line, say whether a request thread is guaranteed to see the whole RateCard, and name the idiom or the missing edge.
(a) static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard(...), read by any thread.
(b) private RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads.
(c) private volatile RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads.
(d) cards.put(id, card) on a ConcurrentHashMap, and request threads call cards.get(id).
try.expect: (a) Safe: the static initializer runs under the class-initialization lock. (b) Not safe: no edge, so a reader may see a half-built card or never see it at all. (c) Safe: volatile write, then volatile read. (d) Safe: putting into a concurrent map happens-before a get that returns it.

sections.h: Final fields survive a data race
sections.html:
The memory model gives final fields one extra promise. The JLS (section 17.5) says, in short: a thread that can only see a reference to an object after its constructor has finished is guaranteed to see the correct values of that object's final fields. No volatile, no lock. It holds even when the reference reached the reader through a data race.

The promise reaches through the field. If a final field points to an array or a map, the reader also sees its contents as they were at the end of the constructor. The JLS calls the end of the constructor the freeze.

Java
final class Quote {
    private final String scheme;            // final: correct even through a race
    private final Map<String, Long> fees;   // final: and the map's contents as of the constructor
    private long hits;                      // plain: a racing reader may see 0

    Quote(String scheme, Map<String, Long> fees) {
        this.scheme = scheme;
        this.fees = Map.copyOf(fees);
    }
}
Kotlin
class Quote(scheme: String, fees: Map<String, Long>) {
    private val scheme = scheme                 // val: a final field, correct even through a race
    private val fees = fees.toMap()             // val: and the map's contents as of the constructor
    private var hits = 0L                       // var: a plain field, a racing reader may see 0
}

In BasicJMM_08_Finals, making all four fields final removed every partial result on both x86_64 and AArch64: readers saw either no object or the complete one.

HotSpot keeps that promise with a barrier. When a constructor writes a final field, the C2 compiler puts a store-store barrier at the end of the constructor: every write before it must complete before any store after it, and the store that publishes the reference always comes after. On x86 the barrier compiles to nothing, because the CPU keeps stores in order anyway; it only stops the JIT from moving stores across it. On ARM it is a real fence instruction.

Two limits. Final fields don't make the reference visible: a reader spinning on a plain field may still never see your object. And the promise holds only if this doesn't escape before the constructor ends: a thread that gets the reference before the barrier gets no ordering at all. The next section shows how that happens.

Put the pieces together and you get an immutable object: a final class, every field final, mutable inputs copied in the constructor, nothing mutable handed out, and no escaping this. You can share it through any race and no reader will ever see it half-built or changing. Java records and Kotlin classes with only val properties get you most of the way. They still store a caller's mutable list as it is, so copy it, for example in a record's compact constructor: record FeeSchedule(List<Fee> fees) { FeeSchedule { fees = List.copyOf(fees); } }.

try.title: Find final in the bytecode
steps: Run both demos below once (the Java one, then the Kotlin one) so Gradle compiles them.
From labs/, run javap -p 'jmm/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo$Quote.class' and the same for FinalFieldsDemo$MutableQuote.class.
Predict before each command: which fields will say final?

code.title: FinalFieldsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l04; /** Where final fields come from in Java. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ public class FinalFieldsDemo { // a record's components become private final fields record Quote(String scheme, long feeCents) {} // for contrast: plain, non-final fields static final class MutableQuote { String scheme; long feeCents; } public static void main(String[] args) { Quote q = new Quote("VISA", 120); MutableQuote m = new MutableQuote(); m.scheme = "MC"; m.feeCents = 135; System.out.println(q + " and a mutable quote for " + m.scheme); } }

alt.title: FinalFieldsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l04 /** Where final fields come from in Kotlin. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ class KQuote(val scheme: String, val feeCents: Long) // val: a private final backing field class KMutableQuote(var scheme: String, var feeCents: Long) // var: a private, non-final backing field fun main() { val q = KQuote("VISA", 120) val m = KMutableQuote("MC", 135) m.feeCents = 140 println("${q.scheme} ${q.feeCents} and a mutable quote for ${m.scheme} ${m.feeCents}") }

try.expect: The record and KQuote both show private final java.lang.String scheme; and private final long feeCents;. MutableQuote and KMutableQuote show the same fields without final, and the Kotlin one also has setters. A Kotlin val and a Java record component become the same thing in bytecode: a final field, with the JMM's final-field promise attached.

sections.h: Don't let this escape the constructor
sections.html:
The freeze happens when the constructor returns. Any code that gets hold of this before then can see the object half-built, and that includes code running on the same thread.

this escapes when a constructor:

  • registers the object as a listener or callback;
  • starts a thread, or submits a task, that uses the object;
  • creates a lambda or inner class that captures this and hands it out;
  • calls a method that a subclass can override.

Here's the first case. The bus replays its last event to every new subscriber, so onEvent runs inside subscribe, before the fields are set:

Java
class ChargebackAlerts implements Consumer<PaymentEvent> {
    private final long thresholdCents;
    private final Pager pager;

    ChargebackAlerts(EventBus bus, long thresholdCents, Pager pager) {
        bus.register(this);                  // the bus calls accept() right here...
        this.thresholdCents = thresholdCents; // ...before these fields are set
        this.pager = pager;
    }

    public void accept(PaymentEvent e) {
        if (e.amountCents() > thresholdCents) pager.page(e);   // NullPointerException on pager
    }
}
Kotlin
class ChargebackAlerts(bus: EventBus, thresholdCents: Long, pager: Pager) : Consumer<PaymentEvent> {
    init {
        bus.register(this)                   // the bus calls accept() right here...
    }
    private val thresholdCents = thresholdCents   // ...before these properties are set
    private val pager = pager

    override fun accept(e: PaymentEvent) {
        if (e.amountCents() > thresholdCents) pager.page(e)   // NullPointerException on pager
    }
}

Kotlin runs init blocks and property initializers in the order you write them, so the same bug is one misplaced init away. And Kotlin's null safety doesn't help: pager is declared non-null and still reads as null.

Moving register to the last line of the constructor is not a fix. The final-field promise is tied to the end of the constructor, and a subclass constructor would still run after it. The fix is to keep constructors to assigning fields, and do the wiring after construction: in a static factory (create, then register), in a start() method, or in a @PostConstruct method that your CDI container calls once the bean is built.

try.title: A thread that starts too early
steps: Read ThisEscapeDemo. The constructor starts a heartbeat thread, then resolves its endpoint, which takes about 50 ms.
Predict both lines of output, then run it.
Fix it: move the thread start out of the constructor into a start() method, and call start() from main after construction. Run it again.

code.title: ThisEscapeDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.jmm.l04; /** A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its fields. */ public class ThisEscapeDemo { static final class HeartbeatSender { private final String endpoint; HeartbeatSender(String endpointName) { Thread beat = new Thread(this::sendHeartbeat, "heartbeat"); beat.start(); // `this` escapes to another thread here... this.endpoint = resolve(endpointName); // ...and this final field is set about 50 ms later } void sendHeartbeat() { System.out.println("heartbeat thread sends to: " + endpoint); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { HeartbeatSender sender = new HeartbeatSender("issuer-gateway"); System.out.println("constructor finished, endpoint = " + sender.endpoint); Thread.sleep(100); } // stands in for a DNS or service-registry lookup static String resolve(String name) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return "https://" + name + ".internal:8443"; } }

alt.title: ThisEscapeDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.jmm.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its properties. */ private class HeartbeatClient(endpointName: String) { val endpoint: String init { thread(name = "heartbeat") { sendHeartbeat() } // `this` escapes to another thread here... endpoint = resolve(endpointName) // ...and this val is set about 50 ms later } fun sendHeartbeat() { println("heartbeat thread sends to: $endpoint") // a non-null String that reads as null } } fun main() { val sender = HeartbeatClient("issuer-gateway") println("constructor finished, endpoint = ${sender.endpoint}") Thread.sleep(100) } // stands in for a DNS or service-registry lookup private fun resolve(name: String): String { Thread.sleep(50) return "https://$name.internal:8443" }

try.expect: The first run prints heartbeat thread sends to: null, then the constructor finishes with the real endpoint. The heartbeat thread ran while the constructor was still resolving. In Kotlin the val endpoint: String is non-null by type and still reads as null. After the fix, the heartbeat prints the real URL: start() happens-before the thread's first action, and the field was set before start().

analogy: Publishing an object is like hanging a new price board in the shop window. Hang it before you've finished writing and a passer-by reads half a board, with blanks where prices should be. Safe publication means hanging it only when it's done, in a window everyone looks through. Final fields are like boards printed at the factory: by the time anyone can see one, it's complete, whichever window it's in. The analogy breaks on escaping this: in a shop you'd notice someone reading over your shoulder, and in Java the reader can be your own constructor's callback, running on the same thread.
world: Watch for constructors that wire things up. A Quarkus bean whose constructor calls scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::refresh, ...) before it has assigned its HTTP client will, now and then, run refresh with a null client. A Kafka listener that registers itself with a listener container from its constructor can receive a record before its deserializer is set. Move that wiring into a @PostConstruct method or an @Observes StartupEvent observer, which CDI calls after the bean is fully constructed. For data, prefer records and val-only Kotlin classes for anything you cache and share: rate cards, issuer configs, BIN tables. Publish each new version with one volatile write.
mistake: The most common mistake is calling a class immutable because its fields are final. private final List<Fee> fees assigned straight from the caller's ArrayList is a final reference to a list the caller can still change. A getter that returns that list lets every reader change it too. The final-field promise covers the list's state at the end of the constructor and nothing after. Copy mutable inputs in (List.copyOf, Map.copyOf), hand out only unmodifiable views, and make the class final so a subclass can't add mutable state.

compare.title: An immutable rate card in Java and Kotlin

java.title: RateCard.java
java.html: public final class RateCard { private final String currency; private final Map<String, Long> feesByScheme; public RateCard(String currency, Map<String, Long> feesByScheme) { this.currency = currency; this.feesByScheme = Map.copyOf(feesByScheme); // our own unmodifiable copy } public String currency() { return currency; } public Map<String, Long> feesByScheme() { return feesByScheme; } // safe to hand out }

kotlin.title: RateCard.kt
kotlin.html: class RateCard(val currency: String, feesByScheme: Map<String, Long>) { // our own copy, behind a read-only type val feesByScheme: Map<String, Long> = feesByScheme.toMap() }

compare.note: Kotlin classes are final by default and a val compiles to a private final field with a getter, so the Kotlin class is three lines. The difference is in the map. Map.copyOf in Java returns a truly unmodifiable map. Kotlin's Map is a read-only interface: toMap() gives you a private LinkedHashMap, and code that casts it to MutableMap could still change it. Inside your own code that's usually fine. If the object crosses a library boundary, wrap it with Collections.unmodifiableMap(...) or build it with Java's Map.copyOf.

worked.title: Publish a config snapshot from a scheduler

steps.say: A Quarkus bean refreshes the card issuer's settings every minute on the scheduler thread. Request threads read them for every call. Sometimes a call goes to the new URL with the old timeout. Find both problems.
steps.code: @ApplicationScoped public class IssuerConfigHolder { @Inject SettingsClient settingsClient; private IssuerConfig config = new IssuerConfig(); // 1. a mutable object in a plain field @Scheduled(every = "60s") void refresh() { // scheduler thread Settings s = settingsClient.fetch(); config.setBaseUrl(s.baseUrl()); // 2. changed in place... config.setTimeout(s.timeout()); // ...one field at a time } public IssuerConfig current() { return config; } // 3. request threads read it }

alt.html: @ApplicationScoped class IssuerConfigHolder(private val settingsClient: SettingsClient) { private var config = IssuerConfig() // 1. a mutable object in a plain property @Scheduled(every = "60s") fun refresh() { // scheduler thread val s = settingsClient.fetch() config.baseUrl = s.baseUrl // 2. changed in place... config.timeout = s.timeout // ...one field at a time } fun current(): IssuerConfig = config // 3. request threads read it }

steps.say: First, the refresh changes one shared object in place, field by field, with no lock, so a request can read the new URL next to the old timeout, a pair that was never configured. Second, nothing publishes config safely: the fields are plain and there is no edge from the scheduler thread to the request threads. Even a full lock around refresh wouldn't help readers that don't take it.
Make the config immutable, build a whole new one on each refresh, and publish it with one volatile write. Readers then always get one consistent snapshot.
steps.code: public record IssuerConfig(String baseUrl, Duration timeout) {} // 1. immutable: final fields, no setters @ApplicationScoped public class IssuerConfigHolder { @Inject SettingsClient settingsClient; private volatile IssuerConfig config = new IssuerConfig("https://issuer.example", Duration.ofMillis(800)); @Scheduled(every = "60s") void refresh() { Settings s = settingsClient.fetch(); config = new IssuerConfig(s.baseUrl(), s.timeout()); // 2. build a new snapshot, 3. publish it } public IssuerConfig current() { return config; } // 4. one consistent snapshot per read }

alt.html: data class IssuerConfig(val baseUrl: String, val timeout: Duration) // 1. immutable: val only @ApplicationScoped class IssuerConfigHolder(private val settingsClient: SettingsClient) { @Volatile private var config = IssuerConfig("https://issuer.example", Duration.ofMillis(800)) @Scheduled(every = "60s") fun refresh() { val s = settingsClient.fetch() config = IssuerConfig(s.baseUrl, s.timeout) // 2. build a new snapshot, 3. publish it } fun current(): IssuerConfig = config // 4. one consistent snapshot per read }

steps.say: Why both changes? The record alone makes every snapshot safe to read even through a race, but a reader might keep an old reference for a long time. The volatile alone publishes the reference, but a mutable object behind it could still change under a reader. An immutable object behind a volatile reference fixes both. One habit completes it: a request calls current() once and keeps that snapshot for the whole call.

lab.title: Fix an escaping constructor and an unsafe publication
steps: Run the tests once. All six fail. The FraudMonitor ones fail with a NullPointerException thrown from inside the constructor.
Make RateCard immutable: a final class, final fields, Map.copyOf in the constructor. Keep the public constructor and methods.
Publish safely in RateCardRegistry. Then think: if RateCard is now immutable, why does the waiting reader still need this change?
Fix FraudMonitor so the bus can't see the monitor before its constructor has finished. create stays the only way to make one.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more.
hints: Map.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy, so feesByScheme() can return the field directly.
Final fields make a RateCard safe to read once a thread has the reference. They do nothing to make the reference itself visible to a thread spinning on a plain field.
In FraudMonitor, the private constructor should only assign fields. Construct the monitor in create, then register it, then return it. EventBus and PaymentEvent are given and need no changes.
lab.done: All six tests in SafePublicationTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: An immutable fee schedule from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write FeeSchedule with a currency and a list of fees, immutable and safe to share through any race. Then write a holder that publishes the latest schedule to request threads. Check: what would break if you skipped the copy?

answer.html: public final class FeeSchedule { // final: no mutable subclasses private final String currency; // final fields: safe through a race private final List<Fee> fees; public FeeSchedule(String currency, List<Fee> fees) { this.currency = currency; this.fees = List.copyOf(fees); // copy in: the caller can't change ours } public String currency() { return currency; } public List<Fee> fees() { return fees; } // unmodifiable: safe to hand out } public final class FeeScheduleHolder { private volatile FeeSchedule current; // volatile: each new schedule is published safely public void replace(FeeSchedule next) { current = next; } public FeeSchedule current() { return current; } } // Without the copy, the caller still holds the list and can change it under every reader.

alt.html: class FeeSchedule(val currency: String, fees: List<Fee>) { // final by default val fees: List<Fee> = fees.toList() // copy in: the caller can't change ours } class FeeScheduleHolder { @Volatile var current: FeeSchedule? = null // each new schedule is published safely private set fun replace(next: FeeSchedule) { current = next } } // Without the copy, the caller still holds the list and can change it under every reader.

recap: Publishing an object is a write of a reference. With no edge, a reader can see the reference before the constructor's writes, or never see it.
Safe publication idioms: a static initializer, a volatile field or AtomicReference, a final field of a properly built object, or a lock or java.util.concurrent handoff.
Final fields are seen as the constructor set them, even through a data race, but they don't make the reference visible.
An immutable object (final class, final fields, copied inputs, no escaping this) is safe to share however it is published.
this escapes when a constructor registers it, starts a thread with it, or hands out a lambda that captures it. Wire objects up after construction.
For data you replace at runtime, publish an immutable snapshot through a volatile reference.

explain.prompt: FraudMonitor had only final fields, yet the bus's replayed event hit a NullPointerException inside it. Explain why, in your own words, and why moving register to the end of the constructor is not the right fix.
explain.answer: The constructor handed this to the bus before it set its fields, and the bus called accept right away to replay its last event. At that point flagged and limitCents still held their default values, null and 0, so flagged.add threw. Final fields don't help, because their promise starts when the constructor returns, and the object was used before that. Moving register to the last line would make this single-threaded case work, but the bus's other threads would still get the object before its constructor finished, with no final-field promise, and a subclass constructor would run even later. The right fix is to only assign fields in the constructor and register the finished object from a factory method.

deeper.html:
The final-field promise has a few edges worth knowing.

It covers what the constructor set and what the final fields point to as of the freeze. Change a mutable object that a final field points to after the constructor, and those later changes get no promise. That's why "effectively immutable" objects (objects nobody changes after publication, though nothing stops them) still need safe publication, while truly immutable objects don't.

Reflection can break final. Frameworks have long used deep reflection (Field.setAccessible(true) followed by set) to write final fields after construction, and the JMM gives such writes almost no guarantees. JDK 26 starts closing this door with JEP 500, "Prepare to Make Final Mean Final": by default it warns when deep reflection mutates a final field, and a later release is planned to make that an error unless you opt in. Serialization libraries and mocking tools are the usual sources of these warnings.

Finally, the static-initializer idiom works because class initialization is itself a synchronization protocol. The JVM initializes each class once, under a lock, and any thread that then uses the class is guaranteed to see what the static initializer wrote. Lesson 5 of this track builds lazy initialization on exactly that.

Aleksey Shipilëv's "Safe Publication and Safe Initialization in Java" separates the two ideas this lesson combines: safe publication (the channel) and safe initialization (final fields), and measures what each costs.
